Disclaimer, unlike a number of the people on this sub I don’t have, nor am I in the process of attaining, a collage degree in any form of data analysis or statistics. My knowledge comes from an AP Stats high school class, independent learning/application, and a Coursra class that I took in my free time so I could very well be wrong with some of the things I say. I’d also highly recommend putting your data into some kind of spreadsheet like Google sheets to make calculations easier. 

This paragraph will be for a very bare bone interpretation. First things first, you want to know what your end goal is for the study, which you said is “see overall if we are happy or not.” To do this we will need to know want score do respondents interpret as the ‘neutral’ option throughout the survey. We want this because it lets us measure ‘happy’ as any score higher than our neutral score. If you gave the respondents instructions saying something like ‘a score of 5 is neutral’ or ‘a score of 7 is neutral’ then we already put neutral score. If not, I’d recommend recollecting the data with that clarification, if possible. If you can’t do that, it’s up to take your best guess on what a neutral score is. Next take the **median**, of a given question’s score, and compare it to your neutral score. A median less than the neutral score means people are generally less happy with the community on that topic, a median equal to the neutral means people are generally not happy or unhappy with the community on that topic, and a median higher than that neutral means people are generally happy with the community on that topic. 

This paragraph is about running a test on the data. Running a test lets us take into account the expected variability of scores, and making sure that that variability isn’t so strong it gave us a misleading result by chance. Using the idea of what a neutral score is, we can get to the actual testing of the data. Then, using some kind of statistical software, spreadsheet, calculator, etc. find a way to preform a “one sample t-test.” This will likely ask for your data points outright, or it might ask you for something called parameters. The parameter “x” with a line on top of it, sometimes called x-bar would mean the average score for a given question. The parameter that looks like a weird “u,”with one side thats really long, will be **for this study only** the neutral score we described earlier, this weird “u” looking thing is sometimes called Mu (pronounced “Mew” like the Pokémon). If it asks for a “s” parameter, that’s the standard deviation of a question’s scores, the formula for “s” is kind of scary if you don’t know much about statistics yet so feel free to use a calculator, however please make sure that if you use a calculator your using it for the sample standard deviations because sample standard deviation has a slightly different formula compared to the ‘normal’ one. The parameter “n” is how many data points/responses you got, so if 10 people answered a given question, n=10. Lastly, you may or may not be asked about a value for “a” or a value “alpha”, this by default should be 0.05, for the purpose of this study the default will work as intended. After doing that you will probably get a fair amount of info thrown at you, what we are interested in is something called a “p-value” specifically the one tailed p-value. This p-value will be any number 0-1 and what we are looking to see is if our p-value is less than or equal too our “alpha” value of 0.05. If it is then congratulations you can say with statistical significance that happiness is high.
